title: THEY WERE UNCLEAN… BUT HAD THEY SINNED? THE SHOCKING TRUTH ABOUT LEVITICUS 15 THAT MANY CHRISTIANS HAVE NEVER BEEN TAUGHT
paragraphs: THEY WERE UNCLEAN… BUT HAD THEY SINNED? THE SHOCKING TRUTH ABOUT LEVITICUS 15 THAT MANY CHRISTIANS HAVE NEVER BEEN TAUGHT

Not everyone declared unclean was guilty of sin. Not every person kept away from God's sanctuary had rebelled against Him. And when you discover why this distinction matters, you may never read the Law of Moses—or the healing touch of Jesus Christ—the same way again.
Imagine waking up one morning and discovering that something happening naturally inside your own body has made you ceremonially unclean.
You haven't stolen anything.
You haven't lied.
You haven't betrayed your spouse.
You haven't deliberately disobeyed God.
Yet according to the Law given to ancient Israel, you must wash, wait, and temporarily observe restrictions concerning sacred things.
Now imagine someone standing nearby, looking at you as though your condition proves that God is angry with you.
You want to explain.
You want to defend yourself.
But how do you convince someone that being unclean is not always the same thing as being sinful?
And here is where the story becomes uncomfortable.
Because thousands of years later, we still have a terrible habit of looking at someone's condition and assuming we know the condition of their soul.
We see sickness and suspect judgment.
We see suffering and imagine punishment.
We see someone's complicated past and quietly conclude that they must have deserved whatever happened to them.
Sometimes we even look at our own struggles and wonder whether God has turned His face away.
But what if we have misunderstood something fundamental about holiness?
What if Leviticus 15, a chapter many Christians skip because its subject matter feels uncomfortable, actually exposes one of our most dangerous spiritual assumptions?
And what if understanding that chapter prepares us to appreciate one of the most breathtaking encounters in the ministry of Jesus Christ?
Stay with me.
Because before we reach the woman who touched the garment of Jesus, we need to understand the Law that shaped the world she lived in.
And once we do, something extraordinary becomes visible.
The God who taught Israel to distinguish between the holy and the common never gave us permission to confuse every human weakness with personal wickedness.
Leviticus 15 begins with a subject that would make many modern congregations uncomfortable if someone read it aloud on Sunday morning.
Bodily discharges.
Male genital discharges.
Semen.
Menstruation.
Abnormal bleeding.
Washing.
Waiting.
Contamination of beds, seats, clothing, and other objects.
And restrictions concerning ritual purity.
It is not the kind of passage people usually print on inspirational coffee mugs.
But Scripture does not become less inspired simply because its subject matter makes us uncomfortable.
In fact, sometimes the passages we avoid contain the distinctions we desperately need.
Leviticus 15:19 states in the King James Version:
"And if a woman have an issue, and her issue in her flesh be blood, she shall be put apart seven days: and whosoever toucheth her shall be unclean until the even."
Read that carefully.
The text identifies a normal bodily process and assigns it a period of ritual uncleanness.
But notice what it does not say.
It does not declare that menstruation itself is an act of rebellion.
It does not say that the woman has committed a moral offense merely because her body is functioning.
It does not instruct her to confess menstruation as though it were theft, adultery, or idolatry.
That distinction matters enormously.
Because ritual uncleanness and moral sin are related to the broader biblical understanding of holiness, but they are not identical categories.
In Hebrew, one of the central words in this chapter is טָמֵא (ṭāmēʾ), meaning "unclean."
Its opposite is טָהוֹר (ṭāhôr), meaning "clean" or "pure."
These words can describe a person's ritual status within Israel's worship system.
They do not automatically tell us whether that person has committed a moral sin.
That is not a modern attempt to soften the Bible.
That is a distinction the biblical text itself requires us to recognize.
Consider Leviticus 15:16:
"And if any man's seed of copulation go out from him, then he shall wash all his flesh in water, and be unclean until the even."
The passage describes an emission of semen and the resulting purification requirement.
The emission itself is not automatically identified as moral wrongdoing.
Similarly, Leviticus 15:18 addresses sexual intercourse between a man and a woman, requiring washing and a period of uncleanness until evening.
Yet Scripture elsewhere honors sexual union within marriage.
Genesis 2:24 presents the union of husband and wife as part of God's created order.
How could a legitimate marital act automatically be treated as moral rebellion merely because it produces a temporary state of ritual uncleanness?
It cannot.
That would confuse two categories the Law does not equate.
And this is where some readers need to reconsider what they have been taught.
A person could be ritually unclean without having committed a moral sin.
Even more strikingly, Numbers 19 describes ritual uncleanness associated with contact with the dead.
Death was a profound source of ritual impurity in Israel's sanctuary system.
Yet tending to the dead could be an act of love, duty, and faithfulness.
A person could perform an honorable responsibility and still need purification before approaching sacred things.
The issue was not always personal guilt.
Sometimes it was ritual status.
Sometimes it was contact with conditions associated with mortality, bodily processes, or the boundaries of sacred worship.
But we must be careful not to swing to the opposite extreme.
Ritual impurity was not meaningless.
It was not imaginary.
And the purification instructions were not optional suggestions to ancient Israel.
God had established real boundaries around His sanctuary.
Leviticus 15:31 explains the seriousness of those boundaries:
"Thus shall ye separate the children of Israel from their uncleanness; that they die not in their uncleanness, when they defile my tabernacle that is among them."
The concern was the holiness of God's dwelling place among His covenant people.
The sanctuary was not ordinary space.
Israel was being taught that approaching the presence of the holy God was not something to treat casually.
The distinction between clean and unclean helped order Israel's worship and communal life around the holiness of the Lord.
And the distinction between moral guilt and ritual impurity did not mean that disobeying God's purification commands was harmless.
For example, Numbers 19:20 warns of serious consequences for refusing required purification.
A state of uncleanness might arise without moral wrongdoing, while knowingly disregarding God's commands concerning that state could itself become disobedience.
That is a crucial distinction.
The condition and the response to the condition were not necessarily the same moral issue.
Now look at something else.
Leviticus 15 does not treat every bodily discharge identically.
Ordinary menstruation is addressed in verses 19–24.
Prolonged or abnormal bleeding is addressed in verses 25–30.
In the latter situation, after the discharge ceases, the woman counts seven days before being clean, and the text then prescribes offerings.
Leviticus 15:30 says:
"And the priest shall offer the one for a sin offering, and the other for a burnt offering; and the priest shall make an atonement for her before the LORD for the issue of her uncleanness."
Some readers see the phrase "sin offering" and immediately assume that the woman must have committed a moral offense by bleeding.
But that conclusion does not follow.
The Hebrew term commonly translated "sin offering" is חַטָּאת (ḥaṭṭāʾt).
Depending on its context, the sacrificial term can also be understood as a purification offering.
This is especially important in Leviticus, where sacrificial rituals address not only personal wrongdoing but also the purification of sacred space and the consequences of impurity.
The offering does not prove that the woman's bodily condition was a deliberate moral sin.
The ritual addresses the impurity in accordance with the sanctuary system God gave Israel.
And the language of atonement must be understood within that system rather than automatically reduced to a confession of individual wrongdoing.
Think about that.

A woman could experience prolonged bleeding, suffer physically, undergo the prescribed purification process, and bring the required offering without the Bible ever identifying the bleeding itself as a wicked choice.
Her body was experiencing a condition.
The Law prescribed a ritual response.
Those are not the same thing as saying her character was corrupt.
And now we arrive at the moment that changes the emotional weight of this entire discussion.
Because centuries later, another woman appears in the Gospel narrative.
She has been bleeding for twelve years.
Not seven days.
Not a few difficult weeks.
Twelve years.
Imagine the exhaustion.
Imagine the uncertainty.
Imagine waking up every morning hoping that today might finally be different.
Imagine spending money on treatment.
Imagine watching other people's lives move forward while your own suffering seems to have no ending.
Mark 5:25–26 tells us:
"And a certain woman, which had an issue of blood twelve years,
And had suffered many things of many physicians, and had spent all that she had, and was nothing bettered, but rather grew worse."
Twelve years.
She had suffered.
She had sought help.
She had spent everything.
And she was getting worse.
Under the purity regulations of Leviticus 15:25, prolonged abnormal bleeding would place a woman in a state of ritual uncleanness for as long as the discharge continued.
That background helps us understand the religious world surrounding her suffering.
But we should not claim more than Scripture tells us.
Mark does not provide a complete account of how her community treated her, whether she was personally shunned, or every restriction she experienced.
We should not invent those details.
The suffering Scripture actually records is already heartbreaking enough.
She was physically afflicted.
She had endured unsuccessful treatments.
Her resources were exhausted.
And her condition had persisted for twelve long years.
Then she heard about Jesus.
Something moved inside her.
Not because she had suddenly found another physician with a promising treatment.
Not because she had enough money left for another consultation.
But because she believed that reaching Jesus could change what no one else had been able to change.
Mark 5:27–28 says:
"When she had heard of Jesus, came in the press behind, and touched his garment.
For she said, If I may touch but his clothes, I shall be whole."
Picture that moment.
The crowd pressing around Him.
The noise.
The movement.
The desperation of someone who had already exhausted every ordinary avenue of hope.
And somewhere among them, a woman reaching out.
One hand.
One touch.
One desperate act of faith.
Then Mark 5:29 declares:
"And straightway the fountain of her blood was dried up; and she felt in her body that she was healed of that plague."
Immediately.
After twelve years of suffering, the bleeding stopped.
But the most beautiful part of the story was still coming.
Jesus stopped.
He asked who had touched His clothes.
The woman came forward, trembling, and told Him the truth.
And Jesus did not respond by declaring that her years of bleeding proved she was morally wicked.
He did not accuse her of having deserved her illness.
He did not treat her suffering as evidence that she was beyond the reach of divine mercy.
Instead, Mark 5:34 records these words:
"Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole; go in peace, and be whole of thy plague."
Daughter.
Not an accusation.
Not a verdict of personal guilt.
A word of tenderness.
A word of belonging.
A word spoken by the Son of God to a woman whose life had been marked by years of suffering.
And the Greek wording makes the encounter even more meaningful.
Jesus says:
Θυγάτηρ, ἡ πίστις σου σέσωκέν σε· ὕπαγε εἰς εἰρήνην.
Thygatēr, hē pistis sou sesōken se; hypage eis eirēnēn.
"Daughter, your faith has made you well; go in peace."
The verb σέσωκέν (sesōken) comes from σῴζω (sōzō), a Greek verb that can mean to save, rescue, or heal, depending on the context.
Here, the immediate context unmistakably includes her physical healing.
The wording also belongs to the broader biblical vocabulary of deliverance.
But we should not use that observation to pretend Mark is explicitly teaching every detail of her eternal spiritual condition.
The passage gives us something powerful enough without exaggeration.
Jesus healed her.
He publicly acknowledged her faith.
He addressed her with dignity.
And He sent her away in peace.
Now ask yourself something.
What does this reveal about the heart of Christ?
The woman approached Him carrying a condition that the Mosaic purity laws identified as ritually unclean.
Yet the encounter ends not with Jesus becoming helpless before her impurity, but with the woman receiving healing through His power.
That is a remarkable picture of the authority of Jesus.
However, we must not misrepresent the passage.
Mark does not explicitly narrate a debate about Leviticus 15 or declare that Jesus was encouraging people to disregard God's Law.
The Gospel's emphasis is on Christ's healing authority and the woman's faith.
Nevertheless, when we read the account against its Old Testament background, the contrast is deeply significant.
Her long-standing condition did not prevent Jesus from healing her.
Her suffering did not make her unworthy of His compassion.
And her need was not greater than His power.
Perhaps someone reading this has been carrying a different kind of burden.
Not twelve years of bleeding.
Maybe twelve years of regret.
Twelve years of unanswered questions.
Twelve years of trying to convince everyone that you're doing fine.
Maybe you have been quietly wondering whether every painful thing in your life is punishment for something you did.
Perhaps someone once used Scripture carelessly and convinced you that your illness, disability, infertility, grief, or emotional exhaustion meant God was displeased with you.
Listen carefully.
The Bible does not give us permission to treat every instance of suffering as proof of a particular personal sin.
Jesus Himself confronts that assumption in John 9.
When His disciples encountered a man blind from birth, they asked:
"Master, who did sin, this man, or his parents, that he was born blind?" (John 9:2, KJV)
They assumed his condition had to be explained by someone's specific wrongdoing.
But Jesus answered:
"Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him." (John 9:3, KJV)
Jesus was not claiming that the man and his parents had never sinned in their lives.
He was rejecting the proposed explanation that this blindness was the result of the particular personal sin the disciples were looking for.
And that distinction matters.
Because there are people who have spent years carrying guilt that God never assigned to them.
They have confused suffering with condemnation.
They have mistaken bodily weakness for spiritual rebellion.
They have allowed other people's assumptions to become the voice they imagine God is using against them.
But Leviticus 15 reminds us that not every state of uncleanness was moral sin.
John 9 reminds us that not every disability is the result of a particular personal transgression.
And Mark 5 reminds us that Jesus meets suffering people with power and compassion.
Yet we must go further.
Because Christianity does not teach that human beings are morally innocent simply because some forms of suffering are not punishments for personal sins.
Scripture is clear.
We all need redemption.
Romans 3:23 declares:
"For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God."
The Gospel does not become beautiful by pretending sin is imaginary.
It becomes beautiful when we understand that sin is real, holiness is real, judgment is real, and God's mercy in Jesus Christ is greater than anything we could have achieved by ourselves.
There is a difference between telling a suffering person, "Your suffering proves you are guilty," and telling a sinner, "Christ offers forgiveness to those who repent and believe."
The first statement may be an unjust accusation.
The second is at the heart of the Gospel.
And this is why we must not reduce Jesus to someone who merely makes hurting people feel accepted.
He is far more than that.
He is the holy Son of God.
He calls sinners to repentance.
He forgives sin.
He restores the broken.
He bears our sins in His own body on the tree (1 Peter 2:24).
He dies and rises again.
He does not simply improve our circumstances.
He reconciles sinners to God.
And that brings us to the deepest connection between Leviticus and the Gospel.
The Old Testament purity laws taught Israel that God's holiness mattered.
They taught that the presence of God was not to be approached carelessly.
They established distinctions between clean and unclean, sacred and common.
But those rituals also belonged to a covenantal system that Christians understand in light of the fulfillment accomplished through Jesus Christ.
Hebrews 9:13–14 draws our attention from the ceremonial purification of the old covenant to the surpassing work of Christ.
It asks how much more the blood of Christ can purify our conscience from dead works to serve the living God.
The Greek word translated "purge" in the King James Version of Hebrews 9:14 is καθαριεῖ (kathariei), from καθαρίζω (katharizō), meaning to cleanse or purify.
The point is not that Israel's earlier worship was worthless.
It is that Christ accomplishes what the old covenant's ritual provisions could not ultimately accomplish: the definitive cleansing of conscience and access to God through His sacrificial work.
The Law revealed the seriousness of holiness.
The sacrificial system pointed toward the need for atonement.
And Jesus Christ, our great High Priest, offered Himself.
Not as one more temporary animal sacrifice.
But as the once-for-all sacrifice whose work is sufficient.
Hebrews 10:14 says:
"For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified."
This is where the Gospel reaches into the deepest places of the human heart.
Because there is a kind of uncleanness that water cannot wash away.
Not the natural bodily processes described in Leviticus 15.
I am talking about actual sin.
The dishonesty we justified.
The bitterness we cultivated.
The lust we entertained.
The cruelty we excused.
The pride we protected.
The forgiveness we refused to extend.
The private compromises nobody else saw.
No amount of pretending can make those things holy.
No religious performance can erase them.
No public reputation can cleanse the conscience.
We need more than better appearances.
We need a Savior.
And the astonishing announcement of the Gospel is that Jesus Christ did not come merely to identify our guilt.
He came to save sinners.
Romans 5:8 declares:
"But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us."
While we were yet sinners.
Not after we successfully repaired ourselves.
Not after we finally became impressive.
Not after we convinced everyone that our past was respectable.
Christ died for us while we were sinners.
That is grace.
Not permission to continue in rebellion.
Not an excuse to ignore holiness.
Not a promise that repentance is unnecessary.
Grace is God's undeserved favor, revealed supremely in Jesus Christ, calling us away from sin and into new life.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that the grace of God trains us to deny ungodliness and worldly lusts and to live godly lives.
Grace does not simply cover our past.
Grace teaches us how to live differently.
And suddenly the theme becomes more than a beautiful sentence.
The scandal may be what you actually did.
Or it may be what others wrongly assumed about you.
The shame may be attached to real sin requiring repentance.
Or it may be attached to suffering that was never evidence of personal guilt.
Wisdom requires us to know the difference.
But in both situations, we need the truth of Jesus Christ.
When we are guilty, we need His forgiveness.
When we are falsely condemned, we need His truth.
When we are suffering, we need His compassion.
When we are proud, we need His correction.
When we are weary, we need His strength.
When we are lost, we need His salvation.
And none of those needs places us beyond His ability to respond.
Maybe that is why this passage matters so much today.
Because religious communities can sometimes become very skilled at identifying what looks unclean while becoming painfully careless about identifying what is actually sinful.
We may condemn the visibly struggling while excusing the respectable hypocrite.
We may avoid someone carrying a painful history while welcoming someone whose pride is simply better dressed.
We may speak harshly about another person's body while ignoring the condition of our own hearts.
But Jesus warned against outward religion that neglects inward holiness.
In Mark 7:20–23, He identifies evil thoughts and actions arising from the human heart as sources of moral defilement.
This teaching does not mean the original purity laws were pointless or evil.
It means that ceremonial categories must not be confused with the deeper problem of moral corruption.
And under the new covenant, Christians do not approach God by reproducing the bodily-discharge purification regulations of Leviticus 15.
We approach the Father through Jesus Christ.
Hebrews 10:19–22 grounds our confidence to draw near in the blood of Jesus, His priestly ministry, and the cleansing He provides.
That does not make holiness less important.
It makes the finished work of Christ infinitely precious.
And perhaps this is the moment for a very personal question.
Have you been condemning yourself for something Scripture does not call sin?
Or have you been excusing something Scripture clearly does call sin?
Those are two very different spiritual dangers.
One requires freedom from false guilt.
The other requires repentance from real guilt.
Both require submission to God's Word.
And both lead us toward the same Savior.
Because Jesus never needed to distort the truth in order to demonstrate compassion.
He could look at a suffering woman and heal her without accusing her of a sin the passage did not identify.
And He could look at sinners and call them to repentance without denying the reality of their wrongdoing.
Truth and mercy were never enemies in Him.
That is the Jesus we must preach.
Not a Christ who condemns every human weakness.
Not a Christ who approves every human desire.
But the crucified and risen Lord, full of grace and truth.
And now, remember the woman again.
Twelve years.
An exhausted body.
Money gone.
Hope repeatedly disappointed.
Then a moment in a crowd.
A hand reaching toward the garment of Jesus.
And one word that must have carried extraordinary tenderness:
"Daughter."
We do not know everything that happened in her life afterward.
The Gospel does not tell us.
But we know what Jesus said to her.
Go in peace.
And that is enough to make us wonder how many people around us are desperate to hear the truth about God without being crushed by assumptions God never made.
Maybe someone in your family needs to hear it.
Maybe a friend has been quietly convinced that their illness means God is punishing them.
Maybe someone who left church years ago still remembers being judged for a condition they never chose.
Or maybe someone you love is hiding genuine sin and desperately needs to discover that repentance is not the end of hope.
It can be the beginning of restoration through Christ.
Please do not let this truth end with you.
And if this challenged something you have believed for years, I would genuinely love to hear from you.
You do not have to reveal private details or explain a painful history publicly.
Sometimes those three words are enough to invite another believer to stand with you in prayer.
Your experience may encourage someone who is struggling to find the words for their own prayer.
Return to it when you study Leviticus.
Read the passages for yourself.
Examine the context.
Test every explanation against Scripture, including this one.
Because the goal is not to make people dependent on an article.
The goal is to help people become more faithful readers of God's Word and more devoted followers of Jesus Christ.
That is also why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not simply to publish emotionally moving messages.
Not to replace your local church, your pastor, or your personal study of the Bible.
But to help believers encounter Scripture seriously, understand the Gospel more deeply, recognize biblical truth, and grow in discipleship.
And I want to speak personally to those who believe this kind of ministry should continue reaching more people.
Every article shared can introduce someone to Scripture.
Every meaningful conversation can encourage someone to seek Christ.

Every person who follows Gospel Warrior helps create another opportunity for biblical teaching to reach a friend, a family member, a struggling believer, or someone who has never seriously considered the Gospel.
And for those who want to help sustain and expand this work, there is another way to participate.
It is not a purchase of forgiveness.
It is not a measure of how much Jesus loves you.
And it should never replace your responsibilities to your family or the faithful financial stewardship of your local church.
Biblically, giving should be voluntary, thoughtful, and sincere.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that God loves a cheerful giver, not one compelled by pressure.
Those products are simply an added expression of appreciation.
Invite someone into a conversation about Scripture.
Encourage a struggling believer.
Pray for those who are suffering.
Help someone find a Bible.
Support faithful Gospel teaching wherever God has placed you.
We glorify Him through faith in Jesus Christ, obedience to His Word, love for our neighbors, generous stewardship, and lives transformed by His grace.
And that is what I pray this ministry will continue pointing people toward.
Not a brand above the Gospel.
Not a personality above Scripture.
Not a movement that asks for loyalty at the expense of biblical truth.
But Jesus Christ, who alone is worthy of our worship.
Now, before you leave, I want you to return to the question that brought us here.
Was every instance of ritual uncleanness a moral sin?
No.
And understanding that answer changes the way we read Leviticus 15.
It teaches us to respect the distinctions God actually made.
It protects us from falsely accusing the suffering.
It prepares us to appreciate the compassion and authority of Jesus.
And it reminds us that the deepest cleansing we need from actual sin is found not in ceremonial washing, but in the saving work of Christ.
Perhaps tonight you need to stop carrying guilt that God never placed upon you.
Or perhaps you need to stop hiding sin that God is calling you to confess.
Do not confuse those two things.
But do not run from Jesus in either situation.
Bring your suffering to Him.
Bring your questions to Him.
Bring your repentance to Him.
Bring your wounded heart to Him.
And trust the Savior who died for sinners and rose again.
First John 1:9 promises that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
That is not permission to remain in darkness.
It is an invitation to walk in the light.
And when you remember the woman in the crowd, remember this:
She reached for Jesus because she needed healing.
He answered with compassion and power.
The story does not tell us that every sickness will disappear immediately when someone believes.
It does tell us that Jesus is worthy of faith, that suffering is not automatically proof of personal guilt, and that no human condition places someone beyond the reach of His sovereign compassion.
So do not measure the heart of God by the cruel assumptions of people who have misunderstood His Word.
Look to Jesus Christ.
Study what He said.
Consider what He did.
And see the grace of God revealed in the Savior who gave Himself for us.
Some of the heaviest chains people carry were never placed on them by God—and some of the deepest sins people hide can only be washed away by the blood of Jesus.
